units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

narration_plan.release: not generated yet (generate right before publication)

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Every router keeps one vector, its best known distance and next hop to each destination, hands it to its neighbors every update interval, and relaxes to the cheapest offer plus the link: Bellman-Ford spread across the routers, settling in L minus one intervals, and counting a dead route up to a finite infinity when a link dies.
units.description: Distance-vector routing against Dijkstra and Floyd-Warshall on 200 random graphs: tables equal on every pair, settled in exactly L − 1 intervals; the failed chain counts 3, 4, 5 … 15 to infinity in 15 intervals where split horizon takes 2; poison reverse still fails the RFC 1058 triangle (565 of 1,000 orders); with no cap, 1,002 and counting.
units.time: O(n) entries per router per update interval to each neighbor; L − 1 intervals to settle, at most n − 2
units.space: O(n) per router: a distance and a next hop per destination
units.baseline: Link-state flooding plus Dijkstra at every router
units.plan_row: Distance-vector routing × Bellman-Ford exchange. Puzzle 193, distributed-systems (problemSlug network-routing, the atlas problem page carrying "Network routing"; sibling live lessons bellman-ford-early-exit, puzzle 34, and dijkstra-binary-heap, puzzle 7). Solution distance_vector_routing_bellman_ford_exchange.py (2.0s, 16,430 bytes, prints OK): a random connected weighted graph generator, a lexicographic (cost, hops) Dijkstra that also counts relaxations, Floyd-Warshall, a BFS hop diameter, a DistanceVector class (lockstep or random asynchronous order; split horizon, poison reverse, triggered updates, infinity cap; counts vectors, entries, and changes including next-hop changes, and the worst transient distance to a watched destination), and a link-state flood followed by a counting Dijkstra per router. ORACLES: (1) 200 random graphs (18.7 routers, 38.4 links): quiet tables equal Dijkstra and Floyd-Warshall on every pair, next hops reach every destination at the referee's cost; busy intervals == L - 1 on 200 of 200 (max L 8, max 7 busy), at most n - 2; DV 5.49 intervals incl. the quiet one, 438 vectors, 9,261 entries per graph, 37 numbers per router; link state floods in exactly the BFS hop diameter (4.14 rounds), 5,794 records, 1,635 relaxations, 114 numbers per router. (2) Chain A-B-C, A-B fails, infinity 16, lockstep: plain 15 intervals, worst 15, 15 changes, trace (3,2),(3,4),(5,4),(5,6)...; split horizon 2 intervals, worst 2 (stale truth); poison reverse 2 / 2; triggered updates 1 interval, worst 15, the same 15 changes (asserted equal); 7.5 minutes at RIP's 30 s; poison reverse over 500 random asynchronous orders: worst 2, no count. (3) RFC 1058 triangle after C-target fails: plain, split horizon, poison reverse all 15 intervals / worst 15 in lockstep (the dead route circles A, B, C one router per interval); 565 of 1,000 random asynchronous orders under poison reverse count to 15 (10.0 intervals each), 435 settle in 2.8. (4) 99 random hop-count meshes losing a router: plain / split / poison all 15.0 intervals and worst 15, entries after the failure 10,626 / 8,789 / 10,626; link state 3.3 flood rounds. (5) No cap: after 1,000 intervals B and C hold (1,001, 1,002) and are still changing. Honest: two AUTHOR CORRECTIONS recorded in the header (the draft expected poison reverse to settle the lockstep triangle in four intervals, the trace showed the dead route circling the three routers to 15, so the page calls poison reverse a two-router fix; and a next-hop change at an unchanged distance now counts as a table change, because under poison reverse it changes what neighbors hear, after a premature quiet left one viz router at infinity). Trimmed to the chunk budget at the coordinator's request: the 100-mesh link-loss sweep was dropped, the estimator reads 18.9 KB (solution 16,430 B, content 16,705 B, narration 12,685 B with 12,047 spoken characters, viz 10,618 B). Cards: self, Link-state routing (algoName), Path-vector routing (algoName), Bellman-Ford (live lesson badge, puzzle 34); all pages verified in dist/algo. neverUse: the vector exchange with no finite infinity on links that fail (1,002 and counting; 15 intervals even with the cap on the chain, the triangle, and 99 of 99 meshes). Contest: 5 rows x 4 columns (intervals to settle, worst distance held, what happens, cost). Figure: the chain's (B, C) staircase to the cap of 16 beside split horizon's drop at intervals 1 and 2; cite Hedrick RFC 1058 (1988) DOI 10.17487/RFC1058, Bellman 1958. Viz DistanceVectorViz: nine routers on a seeded mesh with unit links learn their distance to one amber destination, one lockstep interval per tick, blue next-hop markers, green when equal to a BFS referee; after a three-tick hold a failure strikes (seed-driven variant: destination isolated or one used link cut, plain or poison reverse) and the tables re-route or count the dead route in red to the cap of 16; invariant every tick: estimates at least the truth while building, quiet tables equal the referee (infinity included), build took exactly L - 1 busy intervals, no finite estimate reaches the cap; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks, and 40 seeds with every final ok true across all four variants; stepMs 520, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba (plan 24,362 billable characters, 8 provider requests, $0.730860, approval 6980c209...). units.oneLiner: Treat a graph as charges and springs: every pair repels by k squared over d, every edge pulls by d squared over k with k the ideal edge length, each vertex moves along its net force by at most a temperature that cools linearly to zero, and the resting positions are the drawing: adjacent near, everything else apart, symmetry recovered because the forces carry it.
units.description: Force-directed graph drawing against crossing counts, edge evenness, and a scale-free stress: a 6 x 6 grid from 522 crossings and stress 0.3372 to 0 and 0.0135 in 126,000 pair forces (Kamada-Kawai 0.0125, spectral 0.0166); a 12-cycle convex ten of ten; cooling 3.517 to 0.099 per iteration; the grid-cell cutoff left 114 crossings; K8 at 56 vs 19.
units.time: O(n² + m) per iteration for a fixed number of iterations
units.space: positions and one displacement per vertex
units.plan_row: Fruchterman-Reingold × Force-directed placement. Puzzle 198, graphs (problemSlug graph-layout, the atlas problem page carrying "Graph layout"; sibling live lessons barnes-hut-octree-center-of-mass-approximation 112, annealing-cooling 2). Solution fruchterman_reingold_force_directed_placement.py (1.7 s, prints OK): seeded graph generators (grid, cycle, path, random tree, ring with chords, complete), random and circular layouts, FR on the free plane (k = sqrt(1/n), repulsion k^2/d over all pairs or within grid cells of side 2k, attraction d^2/k, cap t from 0.1 linearly to 0 over 200 iterations), Kamada-Kawai (springs L d_ij, stiffness 1/d_ij^2, one Newton step per vertex per sweep, 60 sweeps), spectral layout (Hall 1970, two Laplacian eigenvectors by deflated power iteration), referees: segment-intersection crossing count, edge-length CV, scale-free stress 1 - cos^2(euclidean, graph distance), cycle convexity, mean corner error at degree-4 vertices. MEASURED: C12 from ten random starts convex and crossing-free 10/10, edge CV mean 0.004 max 0.005, random starts average 13.3 crossings; 5x5 grid unfolded 9/10 random starts, mean corner error 1.5 deg, edge CV 0.090 on the unfolded ones, the circular start left 11 crossings; P12 straightness 0.977 mean, 0.781 min. Quality table, 6x6 grid (36 v, 60 e): random 522 crossings / CV 0.452 / stress 0.3372; circular 135 / 0.703 / 0.2088; FR 0 / 0.110 / 0.0135, 126,000 pair forces, ~46 ms; Kamada-Kawai 0 / 0.012 / 0.0125, 2,160 Newton steps, ~20 ms; spectral 0 / 0.277 / 0.0166, ~17 ms. Random tree n=40: random 235/0.323/0.3227, circular 152/0.587/0.2893, FR 0/0.398/0.0406, KK 0/0.130/0.0305, spectral 0/1.002/0.0666. Ring n=40 + 6 chords: random 313/0.433/0.2874, circular 3/1.466/0.1453, FR 5/0.253/0.0627, KK 2/0.142/0.0528, spectral 8/0.694/0.1034. C40: random 280/0.407/0.3707, circular 0/0/0.0147, FR 1/0.129/0.1604, KK 0/0/0.0147, spectral 0/0/0.0147. Cooling on the 6x6 grid: displacement per iteration 3.517 (first ten) -> 0.09864 (last ten), energy 33.25 -> 5.09 decreasing on 59% of iterations; NEGATIVE no cooling: last-ten displacement 3.600, stress 0.0164, CV 0.235, 0 crossings. Determinism bitwise; circular start on the 6x6 grid: stress 0.1274, 16 crossings. Grid-cell variant at n = 144, 200 iterations: exact 2,059,200 pair forces, ~417 ms, stress 0.0310, 4 crossings; cells 320,227 pair forces, ~106 ms, stress 0.1448, 114 crossings; bucketed repulsion differs from the exact sum by 77.2% of its norm at the random start; 10,296 pairs per iteration, ~5e11 at a million vertices. NEGATIVE dense graphs: K6 10 crossings (min 3, convex 15), K8 56 (min 19, convex 70). AUTHOR CORRECTIONS recorded in the file: the frame clamp (convex 1/10 at CV 0.2 -> free plane 10/10 at 0.005); FR does not beat the circular layout on the 40-cycle (circle optimal); final moves are cap-bound near 3%, not under 1%. Cards: self (Fruchterman-Reingold), Kamada-Kawai, Spectral layout, ForceAtlas2 (all algoName, pages in dist/algo). neverUse: exact all-pairs repulsion at a million vertices or a hard distance cutoff instead (10,296 pairs/iteration at 144, 5e11 at 1e6; the cutoff dropped 77.2% of repulsion and left 114 crossings vs 4). Figure: the two force curves balancing at d = k beside a stress bar chart of the five grid layouts with crossing counts; cite Fruchterman and Reingold 1991 DOI 10.1002/spe.4380211102, Eades 1984, Kamada and Kawai 1989. Viz ForceDirectedViz: seeded grid 4x5 / random tree 18 / ring 16 + 3 chords, random start, four FR iterations per tick (stepMs 90), drawing rescaled to the canvas, temperature bar, crossing count red/green, invariant every tick: every move within the cap, all pairs counted, coordinates finite; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 49 ticks, 0 breaks. units.oneLiner: Give every key one home by hashing it and taking the remainder modulo the shard count: loads as even as a multinomial, no directory, one machine per lookup, and a bill that comes due only when N changes, when the modulo re-homes N/(N + 1) of the data where a ring or jump hash moves 1/(N + 1), and when one hot key needs a salt because no hash can split it.
units.description: Hash partitioning on 16 shards held to the multinomial: chi-square 15.06 against 15 over 100 key sets, heaviest shard 1.09 × mean, 100,000 keys each on one shard at 0.34 µs per route; growing to 17 re-homed 94.2% of keys (theory 94.1%) against 6.4% on a ring and 6.0% with jump hash; a hot Zipf key put its shard at 2.58 × mean until salted (1.19).
units.time: O(1) per route (one hash, one modulo); O(n · N/(N + 1)) keys moved when a shard joins
units.space: O(1) routing state; O(n/N) keys per shard
units.baseline: Range partitioning on the same key
units.plan_row: Sharding × Hash partitioning. Puzzle 199, data-retrieval (problemSlug sharding, the atlas problem page carrying "Horizontal scaling"; sibling live lessons consistent-hashing-virtual-nodes, puzzle 40, and rendezvous-highest-random-weight, puzzle 61). Solution sharding_hash_partitioning.py (2.3 s, prints OK, 21 assertions): a deterministic 64-bit BLAKE2 digest as the hash, the modulo router, a consistent-hashing ring with virtual nodes, jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach 2014), a load counter, and a repeated balance experiment. ORACLES: (1) balance: 100 random key sets of 20,000 keys on 16 shards, chi-square mean 15.06 +/- 0.55 against the multinomial's 15, per-shard sd 33.7 against sqrt(n/N (1 - 1/N)) = 34.2, heaviest shard 1.089 x mean at worst (five-sigma bound asserted); (2) routing: 100,000 keys, loads 6,122 to 6,390 around 6,250, every key found on its home shard and on no other, 0.34 us per route; (3) growth: 16 -> 17 under modulo moves 0.9418 (theory 16/17 = 0.9412, asserted within 0.005), 4 -> 5: 0.804, 8 -> 9: 0.896, 32 -> 33: 0.969 (each within 0.012 of N/(N+1)); doubling 16 -> 32 moves 0.4993 and every mover goes to s + 16; the ring with 100 virtual nodes moves 0.0637 and jump consistent hash 0.0596 (theory 1/17 = 0.0588), every move onto the new node; ring loads after the add 5,290 to 7,113 around 5,882; one point per node leaves the heaviest node at 2.1 to 5.4 x mean over 20 rings; on a 10 TB cluster the modulo moves 9.42 TB against 0.60; (4) skew: 200,000 Zipf requests over 100,000 keys, the hottest key 16,610 requests (8.3%) against a shard mean of 12,500, heaviest shard 2.582 x mean, salting the 13 keys above 1,250 requests into 16 sub-keys each gives 1.190 x; (5) range partitioning: a 1,000-key scan touches 1.013 shards against 16 under hashing, the last 10,000 time-ordered inserts land 100% on one range shard against 7.0% on the busiest hash shard, a query by a non-key attribute fans out to 16 either way; (6) negative example: partitioning user ids by their last digit leaves 6 of 16 shards empty with the heaviest at 1.62 x mean. Two author corrections recorded in the header (one-point ring imbalance guessed at two to three times, measured 2.1 to 5.4; salting only two keys left the third-hottest key's shard at 1.4 x, so the page salts every key above a tenth of the mean). Cards: self, Sharding x Range partitioning (algoName Sharding), Consistent hashing x Virtual nodes (live lesson, puzzle 40), Jump consistent hash; neverUse: a bare modulo on a growing cluster or a last-digit hash. Figure: the move fraction N/(N+1) against 1/(N+1) with the measured dots, beside the Zipf shard loads before and after salting; cites Stonebraker 1986, Karger et al. 1997, DeCandia et al. 2007, Corbett et al. 2012, Lamping and Veach 2014. Viz ShardingViz: keys streaming onto 6 to 9 shards under modulo and onto a ring with 48 virtual nodes, one shard joining at half the keys, moved keys flashed red; invariants every tick (every key on exactly one shard in both schemes, the modulo move within six standard errors of N/(N+1), every ring move onto the new shard); NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 66 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 380, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Slide the template over every window and score each by the correlation coefficient of the two pixel sets, mean removed and variance normalized, so any gain or offset in the lighting still scores exactly one at the true match; read each window's mean and variance from two summation tables in four lookups, floor the variance to refuse flat windows, and fit a quadratic around the peak for the sub-pixel position.
units.description: Template matching by normalized cross-correlation: under a random gain and offset NCC finds the planted 12 × 12 patch 24 of 24 times against SSD 8, SAD 6, raw correlation 22; 6 of 6 at noise σ = 80 where SSD finds 1; summation tables replace 404,496 multiplications with 4,096 and match the direct map to 10⁻¹³; 0 of 6 found at 15° of rotation.
units.time: O(positions × template area) for the dot products; O(1) per window for the mean and variance
units.space: two summation tables of the scene plus the score map
units.plan_row: Template matching × Normalized cross-correlation. Puzzle 200, signal-graphics (problemSlug object-detection, the atlas problem page carrying "Pattern localization"; sibling live lessons hough-transform-parameter-space-voting and fft-cooley-tukey). Solution template_matching_normalized_cross_correlation.py (5.9 s, prints OK): texture generator, bilinear warp (shift, rotation, scale), direct per-window scorer returning NCC, SSD, raw correlation, and SAD from shared window sums, two summation tables, a counting radix-2 FFT, Lewis's fast NCC (tables plus FFT numerator), and a 3 x 3 least-squares quadratic sub-pixel fit; 64 x 64 scenes, 12 x 12 pattern planted at a known position, 2,809 candidate positions, seeded. ORACLES: (1) NCC = 1.000000 (within 1e-9) at six exact copies and |NCC| <= 1 on every map (max 1.000000000); exact copies found 24/24 by all four scores; (2) gain 0.4 to 2.5 and offset +-60 on the scene: NCC 24/24, SSD 8/24, SAD 6/24, raw correlation 22/24; (3) additive noise sigma 15/40/80/120: NCC 6,6,6,5 of 6; SSD 6,6,1,0; SAD 6,6,0,1; raw 6,6,2,0; (4) the table-plus-FFT map equals the direct map to 1.2e-13 with its argmax on the plant; direct 404,496 numerator + 404,496 denominator multiplications per match; tables 4,096 (one squared image); FFT numerator 1,441,792 (three 128 x 128 transforms at four real multiplications per complex one), so the FFT costs more than the direct dot products at this size; (5) sub-pixel: integer peak error 0.640 px, quadratic fit 0.314 px over 16 planted fractional shifts; (6) rotation of the planted pattern, hits of 6 (mean peak): 0 deg 6 (1.00), 5 deg 6 (0.98), 10 deg 6 (0.91), 15 deg 0 (0.85), 20 deg 1 (0.76), 30 deg 0 (0.64), 45 deg 0 (0.49); scale 0.8/0.9/1.0/1.1/1.25: 6/6 at every scale; (7) untextured template without the variance floor: 0/6 found, mean peak 0.26; with the floor flagged 6/6; a flat 20 x 20 scene block floors exactly its 81 windows. Three author corrections recorded in the header: the draft assumed the FFT numerator would cut the multiplication count (counters said the opposite); the draft's smooth scenes let chance windows correlate at 0.83 and beat half-pixel-shifted plants (scenes given finer texture, chance peaks 0.44); the draft's two one-dimensional parabolas (0.61 px) were replaced by the 3 x 3 quadratic (0.36 px on the same seed). Cards: self, Phase correlation, SIFT, Hough transform (live lesson badge), all algoName pages present in dist/algo. neverUse: NCC for a rotated object (6/6 at 10 deg, 0/6 at 15 deg) or a texture-free template (0/6, peak 0.26 without the floor). Contest: 6 rows (NCC tables, NCC direct, NCC FFT numerator, SSD, SAD, raw correlation) x 4 columns (exact copy, gain + offset, noise sigma 80, multiplications per match). Figure: hits under lighting change by score, beside multiplications per match on a log scale; cite Lewis 1995, Briechle and Hanebeck 2001 (DOI 10.1117/12.421129), Brunelli 2009. Viz TemplateMatchingViz: a 40 x 40 scene with an 8 x 8 planted pattern shown under a seeded gain (0.4 to 2.2) and offset (+-60) plus noise, one row of 33 windows scored per tick by NCC and SSD, the NCC map filling in blue, the plant in green, the SSD minimum in amber (wrong in 10 of 40 cycles, NCC right in 40 of 40); invariant every NCC inside [-1, 1] and the final peak on the plant; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 32 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 140, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Draw from a proposal that lands on the rare event, weight every sample by the target-to-proposal density ratio, and the weighted average stays unbiased while its variance drops by thousands: the exponential tilt N(4, 1) estimates P(Z > 4) to 1.75% in 10,000 draws where 100,000 plain draws manage 49%, and Kish's effective sample size tells you when the proposal has failed.
units.description: Importance sampling for P(Z > 4) = 3.167e-5 against the exact tail and its closed-form second moment: the tilt N(4,1) cuts per-sample variance 6,999x, matching the formula to 0.2%, ESS 18% of n; an overshooting proposal N(7, 0.5) reports 0.036 of the truth with a 4% spread; stratified 12.4x, control 2.7x, antithetic 2.4x.
units.time: O(n) density ratios per estimate, one pass for ESS
units.baseline: Plain Monte Carlo at ten times the draws
units.plan_row: Importance sampling × Variance-reducing proposal. Puzzle 201, probabilistic (problemSlug variance-reduction, the atlas problem page carrying "Rare-event estimation"; sibling live lesson monte-carlo-integration-uniform-sampling, puzzle 182). Solution importance_sampling_variance_reducing_proposal.py (0.9 s, prints OK): tilted sampling runs returning estimate, second moment, Kish ESS, top-weight share, and the self-normalized estimate; plain Monte Carlo; a bump integrand with closed-form integral and its zero-variance proposal; five estimators of E[exp Z]. ORACLES: P(Z > 4) = 0.5 erfc(4/sqrt 2) = 3.1671e-5 to nine digits; the shifted estimator's exact second moment exp(mu^2) Qbar(a + mu); the zero-variance proposals' constant weights; closed-form variances of the plain estimators. MEASURED (20 runs each): plain n = 100,000 mean/truth 0.979, sd/truth 0.490; tilt N(4,1) n = 10,000 mean/truth 1.001, sd/truth 0.0175, ESS 0.182 n, top weight 0.11%; second moment 5.515e-9 vs exact 5.528e-9 (0.2%); per-sample variance ratio 6,999; best shift mu* = 4.12 (variance 4.485e-9 vs 4.525e-9 at 4); wide N(4,2) sd/truth 0.029, ESS 0.09; undershot N(2,1) 0.066, ESS 0.02; narrow N(4,0.5) 0.015, ESS 0.35 (infinite variance in theory: x^2 coefficient of log(p^2/q) = +1.0, weights pass one beyond x = 8.09, reached once in 6.5e15 draws); overshoot N(7,0.5) mean/truth 0.036, sd/truth 0.041, top weight 64%, ESS 0.0003 n (3 of 10,000); self-normalized tilt 1.89x truth; bump integral 4.62859e-3: plain sd/truth 0.118 (closed form 0.114), N(3,0.5) proposal 0.0086, zero-variance weights constant to 1.3e-17; self-normalized bias with N(3,1): +1.157 (n = 100), +0.394 (1,000), +0.042 (10,000); E[exp Z] = 1.6487 variance ratios antithetic 2.4, control 2.7, stratified (100 strata) 12.4, importance with N(1,1) exact (zero variance). Two author corrections recorded in the header: the narrow proposal expected to blow up was the steadiest row (the divergence lives beyond x = 8.09, never visited), and the self-normalized bias expected to be small was near double. Cards: self, Stratified sampling (12.4x), Control variates (2.7x), Cross-entropy method (qualitative). neverUse: the overshooting proposal, precisely wrong at 0.036 of the truth with a 4% error bar. Figure: target and tilted proposal densities with the event and the weight curve on a log scale, beside a log-scale bar chart of sd/truth for six estimators; cite Kahn and Marshall 1953 (DOI 10.1287/opre.1.5.263), Siegmund 1976 (DOI 10.1214/aos/1176343541), Owen 2013 chapter 9. units.oneLiner: Route every packet by the most specific prefix that covers its destination: store the prefixes in a binary trie keyed by address bits, walk the destination one bit per level remembering the last prefix passed, and answer in at most 32 steps where a scan compares the whole table, with strides for speed and path compression for memory as the measured rivals.
units.description: Longest prefix match on 2,000 seeded prefixes (570 nested) held to a scan of every prefix on 2,200 destinations with 1,200 boundary probes: the unibit trie answers in 17.0 steps mean, 32 max, at 0.60 µs against the scan's 104.3; a stride-8 trie in 2.64 steps from 524,032 entries; Patricia in 3,504 nodes; exact-match hashing misses 1,000 of 1,000.
units.time: O(W) bit steps per lookup (W = 32), independent of the table size; O(W) per insert or delete
units.space: O(total prefix bits) nodes; 20,804 for 2,000 routes, 3,504 path-compressed
units.baseline: Linear scan of every prefix per packet
units.plan_row: Longest prefix match × Trie lookup. Puzzle 202, distributed-systems (problemSlug packet-forwarding, the atlas problem page carrying "IP forwarding"; sibling live lesson trie-shared-prefix-branching, puzzle 51). Solution longest_prefix_match_trie_lookup.py (0.9 s, prints OK): a seeded IPv4 forwarding table with a BGP-like length mix (2,000 prefixes, 570 nested inside a shorter one, 23 distinct lengths, a /0 default), the linear-scan referee, a unibit trie with insert/delete/lookup, a stride-8 multibit trie with controlled prefix expansion, a Patricia trie built from the unibit trie, binary search on prefix lengths with markers (Waldvogel et al. 1997), and a timing harness. ORACLES: (1) all four structures equal the scan on 2,200 destinations (1,000 random plus the first and last address of 300 prefixes and the addresses just outside; 174 destinations covered by two or more prefixes), and again after 200 inserts and 200 deletes (20,978 nodes after, exactly 20,804 after undoing); (2) depth: unibit mean 17.0, max 32 (asserted <= 32); stride-8 mean 2.64, max 4 (asserted <= 4); Patricia 10.8 visits, max 15; length search 4.7 probes, max 5, 2,620 markers over 23 lengths; (3) expansion: 38,625 expanded entries equal the formula sum over prefixes of 2^(8 - len mod 8) - 1; 2,047 nodes x 256 = 524,032 entries against 41,608 unibit slots; Patricia 3,504 nodes asserted fewer than unibit; (4) timings in Python: scan 104.3 us, unibit 0.60, stride-8 0.25, Patricia 0.81, length search 0.42 per lookup; scan = 173x the trie; a 10 GbE line card at 14.88 Mpps has 67 ns per packet, so the scan costs 1,552 budgets and the trie 9; (5) negative example: an exact-match hash table keyed by network addresses misses 1,000 of 1,000 random destinations. Two author corrections recorded in the header (path compression cut nodes sixfold, not by half; the Patricia lookup is slower than the bit walk in Python, 0.81 against 0.60 us, so the page credits memory, not speed). Cards: self, Multibit trie forwarding x Controlled prefix expansion, Radix tree x Path compression (Patricia), Trie x Shared-prefix branching (live lesson, puzzle 51); neverUse: an exact-match hash table or a per-packet scan. Figure: a five-bit trie with a highlighted longest-match walk beside measured steps-per-lookup bars with entry counts; cites Fuller et al. RFC 1519 (1993), Sklower 1991, Degermark et al. 1997, Waldvogel et al. 1997, Srinivasan and Varghese 1999. units.oneLiner: Keep a stack of the symbols still to match and look at one token: compute nullable, FIRST, and FOLLOW as least fixpoints, enter each production under the tokens that can begin it (and, when it can vanish, under the tokens that can follow it), and parse by one table lookup per expansion; a cell with two entries is the proof that the grammar is not LL(1) yet.
units.description: LL(1) parsing from a first-follow table: FIRST and FOLLOW equal the textbook sets, 13 cells, 0 conflicts; 1,500 sentences parse at 5.58 stack ops per token, recursive descent and Pratt agreeing on every tree; 1,248 corruptions rejected at the viable prefix (Earley agrees on all); the left-recursive grammar's 4 conflicts loop on 300 of 300.
units.time: O(n) stack operations, one table lookup per expansion; the table is three fixpoints over the grammar
units.space: the stack (bounded by the parse tree's frontier) plus the table
units.baseline: Hand-written recursive descent for the same grammar
units.plan_row: LL(1) parsing × First-follow table. Puzzle 203, languages-compilers (problemSlug context-free-parsing, the atlas problem page carrying "Predictive parsing"; sibling live lessons pratt-parsing-binding-powers (113) and shunting-yard-operator-stack (174)). Solution ll1_parsing_first_follow_table.py (0.2 s, prints OK): a Grammar class computing nullable, FIRST, and FOLLOW as three least fixpoints with pass counts; the LL(1) table builder recording each conflict as first/first or first/follow; a table-driven parser with an explicit stack building the parse tree and counting lookups and stack operations (with a pick rule for conflicted cells and a step cap); a seeded sentence generator; a one-token corruptor (delete, insert, swap); an Earley recognizer that also reports the longest viable prefix; a hand-written recursive descent parser counting calls; a Pratt parser whose left-associative operator tree the folded LL(1) tree must equal. ORACLES: (1) textbook expression grammar (E -> T E', E' -> + T E' | eps, T -> F T', T' -> * F T' | eps, F -> ( E ) | id): nullable {E', T'}, FIRST and FOLLOW equal Aho/Lam/Sethi/Ullman 4.4 exactly, 13 table cells, 0 conflicts, fixpoint passes 2, 4, 3; (2) 1,500 generated sentences (17,800 tokens, longest 41): all accepted, every tree re-yields its string, recursive descent agrees with 37,184 calls = the 37,184 table lookups (one per expansion), the folded tree equals the Pratt tree on all 1,500; (3) 1,500 corruptions: 1,248 rejected, Earley agrees on all 1,500 and recursive descent too, every LL(1) error position equals the longest viable prefix (correct-prefix property); (4) work: stack ops = 5.58 x tokens + 9.0, every parse within 16 ops of the line, max 14 ops per token (one-token input), asserted under 20 residual and under 15 per token; Earley 78,715 chart items (4.4 per token) and 3x the LL(1) time on the corruptions; (5) left-recursive grammar E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F: 4 FIRST/FIRST conflicts (E and T on id and '('); the transformed grammar agrees with Earley on the original on 1,200 strings both ways; fed directly, preferring the recursive production loops (step cap) on 300 of 300 valid inputs, preferring the other rejects 252 of 300 (every input containing + or *); (6) dangling else S -> if c then S S' | other, S' -> else S | eps: exactly 1 FIRST/FOLLOW conflict on (S', else); preferring 'else S' binds the else to the innermost if at depths 1 to 6 on 6 nestings, preferring eps rejects all 6; S -> a b | a c: 1 conflict, left-factored 0. AUTHOR CORRECTION recorded in the header: the draft asserted every parse within three slopes of the linear fit; one-token inputs sit 16 ops off the line, so the page states the measured bound. Cards: self (algoName LL(1) parsing), Recursive descent parsing, LALR parsing x Merged lookahead states, Pratt parsing x Binding-power dispatch (live lesson badge); all pages exist in dist/algo. neverUse: the left-recursive grammar fed straight to the LL(1) parser (4 conflicts; loops on 300 of 300 or rejects 252 of 300). Contest: conflicts / valid accepted / corruptions rejected / work per token for the LL(1) table, recursive descent (2.09 calls per token), Earley (4.4 items, 3x time), and LL(1) on the left-recursive grammar. units.oneLiner: Take any edge with neither end chosen, put both ends in the cover, delete what they touch, repeat: the kept edges are a maximal matching, every cover needs one vertex per kept edge, so the output is at most twice the optimum in one linear pass, with the matching as a receipt; the max-degree greedy beats it on average and loses by a logarithm when the graph is chosen against it.
units.description: The maximal-matching rule against exact optima on 300 random graphs: 1.495 × OPT mean, 2.000 worst, |M| ≤ OPT ≤ 2|M| on every graph; K6,6 and a star return exactly 2 × OPT; the max-degree greedy averages 1.032 but climbs 2.125, 2.719, 3.375, 4.039 on the bad family at n = 16 to 128 (OPT by Kőnig) while the matching rule stays at 2.000.
units.time: O(V + E): one pass over the edges
units.space: O(V) for the cover and the matching
units.baseline: Max-degree greedy (greedy set cover on edges)
units.plan_row: Greedy vertex cover × Maximal matching. Puzzle 204, optimization-or (problemSlug vertex-cover, the atlas problem page carrying "Vertex cover 2-approximation"; sibling live lessons greedy-set-cover-max-coverage, branchbound-fractional, hopcroft-karp-layered-phases). Solution greedy_vertex_cover_maximal_matching.py (1.0 s, prints OK): the matching rule, the max-degree greedy with incremental degrees, exact branch and bound (branch on the max-degree vertex, prune with the matching bound), brute force for small graphs, Kuhn's augmenting-path matching, Konig's cover from the matching, the half-integral LP solved through the bipartite double cover with a dual fractional matching as the optimality certificate, and the generator for the degree greedy's bad family. ORACLES: (1) exact solver equals brute force on 60 graphs of 6 to 11 vertices; (2) 300 random G(14, 0.3) graphs: matching rule 1.495 mean / 2.000 worst against OPT (15 branch-and-bound nodes mean), |M| <= OPT <= 2|M| and a valid cover on every graph; degree greedy 1.032 / 1.286; LP rounding at one half 1.757 / 2.000; OPT/LP 1.123 mean; primal feasible, dual feasible, values equal on every graph; (3) edge order: one order 1.491 against best of eight shuffles 1.289 (40 graphs); (4) tight examples: K6,6 cover 12 against OPT 6 (ratio 2.0, degree greedy optimal at 6), star K1,8 cover 2 against 1; (5) Konig: min cover = max matching = brute force on 40 random bipartite graphs; (6) bad family (n left vertices; for each i in 2..n, n // i right vertices of degree i): OPT = n exactly by Konig; degree greedy takes every right vertex, 34 / 87 / 216 / 517 at n = 16 / 32 / 64 / 128, ratios 2.125 / 2.719 / 3.375 / 4.039 against H_n - 1 = 4.433 at 128; matching rule 2.000 on each; (7) exact search at average degree 4: 24 / 118 / 919 / 4,514 / 31,496 nodes at n = 24 / 48 / 72 / 96 / 120 (asserted > 100x growth). Two author corrections recorded in the header: the draft guessed the matching rule's worst case over random graphs at 1.90 and measured exactly 2.00; the draft expected branch and bound to blow up by n = 24 on dense random graphs, where the matching bound prunes to a few dozen nodes, so the growth experiment moved to sparse graphs. Cards: self, LP rounding vertex cover (algoName), Greedy set cover (max-degree greedy, live lesson badge), Branch and bound (live lesson badge). neverUse: the max-degree greedy when the graph may be chosen against you (the bad family ratios). Figure: mean and worst ratios for three methods beside the bad-family ratio climbing with n against the matching rule's flat 2.000; cite Gavril in Garey and Johnson 1979, Karp 1972, Khot and Regev 2008 (DOI 10.1016/j.jcss.2007.06.019), Konig 1931.
